stem: Kellogg's added two new products to its already broad and well-established brands of breakfast cereals. Because Kellogg's was widely recognized and known for high quality, these products required little or no learning by the customers and achieved sales exceeding 3 million units in the first quarter of their availability. Adding these new products to the range of existing ones is known as:
explanation: A line extension is the addition of a new item to an already existing product line, here two new cereals under well-known Kellogg's brands. Harvesting is the opposite move (cutting support for a declining product), and test marketing is a limited trial, not adding items to a line.

stem: The addition of a new item, such as a flavour, size or variety, to an already existing product line is a(n) _____.
explanation: That is a line extension. A brand extension is different: it moves an existing brand name into a NEW product class (Chapter 7) rather than adding an item within the same line.

stem: Which scenario is a line extension rather than a brand extension?
options: A cereal brand launches a line of frozen pizzas under its name
A running-shoe brand launches branded energy drinks
Banff Tea Co. adds a chai variety to its bagged-tea line
A toothpaste brand launches branded razors
explanation: Adding a new variety within the same product line (bagged tea) is a line extension. The other three take an existing brand name into a new product class, which is a brand extension.

stem: Why do line extensions launched under a well-known brand often sell quickly?
options: Consumers already know and trust the brand, so little learning is required
Line extensions are radical innovations that create primary demand
Line extensions skip the introduction stage because they are test marketed
Line extensions are priced using a harvesting strategy
explanation: A trusted brand name carries over to the new item, so buyers understand and accept it immediately, as with Kellogg's new cereals. Line extensions are typically minor, low-learning additions, not radical innovations.

stem: Nordik Granola's best-selling granola is in maturity. Its manager wants a fast, relatively low-risk way to refresh the brand on the shelf while using the trust the brand has already earned. Which tactic fits best?
options: Diversify into a new product for a new market
Delete the granola from the line
Run a controlled test market of the existing granola
Add new flavours to the existing line
explanation: A line extension (new flavours in the existing line) is a classic maturity tactic that uses brand trust to refresh the line. Diversification is the riskiest growth path, and deletion abandons the product rather than refreshing it.

stem: The slide asking 'Why all the varieties? Good idea?' about Tide's many line extensions suggests that adding too many varieties can backfire by confusing consumers and cannibalizing the brand's existing items.
explanation: True. Line extensions keep a mature brand fresh, but too many varieties can confuse shoppers and pull sales from the brand's own existing items (cannibalization) rather than from competitors.

stem: When a firm's new product takes sales away from the firm's own existing products, this is called:
explanation: Cannibalization means the new product 'eats' the firm's own sales. Market penetration is tempting, but it refers to growing a current product's sales among current customers, often at competitors' expense.

stem: After Lakeshore Dairy launched a premium lactose-free milk, its overall milk sales barely changed: most buyers had simply switched from Lakeshore's regular lactose-free milk. This is an example of:
explanation: Sales shifted from Lakeshore's existing product to its own new product, which is cannibalization. It is not the decline stage, because the drop was caused by the firm's own launch, not by outside technology or environmental change.

stem: Sales of Oakridge's original sports drink fell 15% last year. Which explanation indicates cannibalization rather than the decline stage?
options: Consumers switched to a new rival technology
Oakridge cut advertising to harvest the product
Customers switched to Oakridge's own new zero-sugar version
explanation: Cannibalization is when the firm's OWN new product takes sales from its existing product. A shrinking category or a rival technology points to decline, and cutting advertising describes harvesting.

stem: Why is cannibalization a particular concern when a brand adds many line extensions?
options: New items in the line mostly draw buyers from the brand's existing items, not from rivals
Line extensions require radical new learning and consumption patterns by consumers
Line extensions always shrink the brand's distribution and shelf space
Line extensions automatically move the brand into a brand-new market
explanation: Because line extensions are close substitutes for the brand's existing items, many buyers simply switch within the brand, so total sales grow little. Line extensions are typically low-learning additions, not radical innovations.

stem: Which outcome would NOT be described as cannibalization?
options: A competitor's new cereal takes sales from a firm's cereal
A new flavour of a firm's yogurt pulls buyers from its original flavour
A firm's new tablet reduces sales of its own laptops
A firm's new mini size reduces sales of its regular size
explanation: Cannibalization only happens when a firm's own new product takes its own sales. Losing sales to a competitor's product is ordinary competition, not cannibalization.

stem: Suzanne's Soup Company noticed that people only ate soup for lunch, so they added recipes to the back of the labels to encourage people to use their soups to make dinner too. This is an example of:
explanation: Creating a new use situation means finding a new occasion or use for an existing product, here dinner instead of only lunch. Product improvements is wrong because the soup itself did not change; only the occasion being promoted did.

stem: Petal & Pine, maker of a gentle baby shampoo, launches ads suggesting that adults with sensitive scalps use the same shampoo. This market modification is:
explanation: The product and its use (washing hair) are unchanged; the firm is targeting a new group of buyers, adults, so this is finding new customers. It is not a new use situation, because the shampoo is still used for the same purpose.

stem: Polar Fizz, a sparkling-water brand, runs a campaign encouraging its current drinkers to have three cans a day instead of one. This market modification is:
explanation: Getting existing customers to use the product more often or in larger amounts is increasing a product's use. It is not a new use situation, because the drink is used the same way, just more frequently.

stem: Which pairing correctly matches a market modification with its example?
options: New use situation: promoting baking soda as a fridge deodorizer
Increasing use: marketing a women's razor to men
Finding new customers: label recipes encouraging soup at dinner
New use situation: asking current users to apply sunscreen twice as often
explanation: Baking soda used to deodorize a fridge is a new purpose, so it is a new use situation. A razor marketed to men is finding new customers, soup recipes for dinner are a new use situation, and applying sunscreen more often is increasing use.

stem: Market modification extends a product's life cycle by:
options: improving the product's quality or adding line extensions to it
trading the product up or down to change the value it offers
finding new customers, increasing a product's use, or creating new use situations
deleting the product or harvesting it to reap remaining profits
explanation: Market modification changes the market, not the product: new customers, more use, or new use situations. Improving the product or adding line extensions is product modification.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a market modification?
options: Adding a new flavour to the line
explanation: Adding a new flavour is a line extension, which is a product modification. The other three change who uses the product or how it is used, so they are market modifications.

stem: Hearth Oats' rolled oats are bought almost only for breakfast porridge. Management wants growth without changing the product or targeting a new group of customers. Which tactic fits?
options: Launch a gluten-free oat line (a line extension)
Promote oats as an ingredient in baking and smoothies (a new use situation)
Target university students who don't buy oats (finding new customers)
Upgrade quality and raise the price (trading up)
explanation: Promoting oats for baking and smoothies gives current customers a new occasion to use the unchanged product, which is creating a new use situation. Targeting students would be finding new customers, which management ruled out, and a gluten-free line changes the product.

stem: According to the slides, a firm repositions a product in order to:
options: reduce a large list of new-product ideas to a manageable number
meet changing consumer needs, react to competition, or improve value
test the marketing mix on a limited scale in a defined area
reap minor profits while cutting the product's marketing support
explanation: The slides list three reasons to reposition: meet changing consumer needs, react to competition, or improve value. Reaping minor profits while cutting support is harvesting, a decline strategy rather than an extension strategy.

stem: Fernwood Candles upgrades its existing basic candles with hand-poured soy wax, designer jars and essential oils, and raises their price by 60%. This is:
explanation: Adding value and features to the existing product and raising its price is trading up, a repositioning tactic. It is not a line extension, because Fernwood upgraded its existing candles rather than adding a separate new item to the line.

stem: Without changing the price, Crispo Chips reduces its bag from 235 g to 200 g. In PLC repositioning terms, this is:
explanation: Trading down includes reducing features, quality or price, and also downsizing package contents while keeping the price the same. It is not a product improvement, because consumers get less product rather than a better one.

stem: What is the difference between trading up and trading down?
options: Trading up lowers the price to gain volume; trading down raises the price to signal quality
Trading up targets new customers; trading down targets the firm's current customers
Up adds value or features and raises price; down cuts features, quality, price or package size
Trading up is a market modification; trading down is a product modification
explanation: Trading up = more value for a higher price; trading down = less (fewer features, lower quality, a lower price, or smaller contents at the same price). Both are repositioning moves, not market or product modifications.

stem: Hinterland Outfitters repositions its rugged work boots as stylish urban footwear after noticing young city shoppers adopting the look. Which reason for repositioning does this best illustrate?
options: Catching a rising trend to meet changing consumer needs
Reducing cannibalization of its line extensions
Preparing the boots for test marketing
explanation: Firms reposition to meet changing consumer needs, react to competition or improve value, which includes catching a rising trend like urban workwear. Skimming is an introduction-stage pricing strategy and has nothing to do with repositioning an established product.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of repositioning?
options: A budget hotel chain upgrades its rooms and raises its rates
A cereal maker shrinks box contents but keeps the same price
A juice brand moves from a kids' image to an adult health image
A juice brand adds a new mango flavour to its line
explanation: Adding a new flavour to the line is a line extension (product modification). Upgrading with higher rates is trading up, shrinking contents at the same price is trading down, and moving from a kids' to an adult image changes the product's position, so all three are repositioning.

stem: Dr. Oetker, a popular frozen pizza brand, regularly adds new pizza types and flavours to its existing product mix. In terms of new product innovation, launching new pizza flavours is a/an:
explanation: Minor innovations are small product modifications that require no adjustment or new learning by consumers; nobody needs to be taught how to eat a new pizza flavour. 'Continuous improvement' sounds like the real term, but even a true continuous innovation would change the consumer's routine, which a new flavour does not.

stem: An innovation that changes the consumer's normal routine but does not require totally new learning is a:
explanation: That is a continuous innovation, such as the Swiffer WetJet. A radical innovation goes further and requires new learning and new consumption patterns.

stem: Driverless delivery pods will require Canadians to learn new ways of receiving packages and to adopt entirely new consumption patterns. In terms of degree of innovation, the pods are a:
explanation: Requiring new learning and new consumption patterns is the definition of a radical innovation, like self-driving cars in Figure 8-5. A continuous innovation changes routines but does not demand totally new learning.

stem: Lumio is launching a home 3D food printer, a radical innovation. According to Figure 8-5, its marketing emphasis should be to:
options: gain consumer awareness and achieve wide distribution in many stores
advertise its points of difference and benefits versus competitors
educate consumers via advertising, product trial, personal selling and PR
use very low prices and keep promotion to a minimum, if any
explanation: Radical innovations need consumer education through advertising, product trial and personal selling, and public relations can play a major role. Gaining awareness and wide distribution is the emphasis for minor innovations, which require no learning.

stem: SparkleBright is launching a new and improved version of its toothpaste. Per Figure 8-5, what should its marketing emphasize?
options: Gaining consumer awareness and wide distribution
Educating consumers through personal selling and product trial
Public relations to explain new consumption patterns
Advertising that teaches consumers a new daily routine
explanation: New and improved toothpaste is a minor innovation requiring no new learning, so the emphasis is awareness and wide distribution. Personal selling, product trial and PR-led education are for radical innovations.

stem: Which pairing of innovation type and marketing emphasis is correct?
options: Minor innovation: educate consumers through personal selling
Radical innovation: gain consumer awareness and wide distribution
Continuous innovation: use public relations to teach entirely new consumption patterns
Continuous innovation: advertise points of difference and benefits to consumers
explanation: Figure 8-5 pairs continuous innovation with advertising points of difference and benefits. The other options scramble the table: personal selling and PR-led education belong to radical innovation, and awareness plus wide distribution belongs to minor innovation.

stem: Which example is NOT listed as a radical innovation in Figure 8-5?
explanation: The Swiffer WetJet is Figure 8-5's example of a continuous innovation: it changes the cleaning routine without requiring totally new learning. Self-driving cars, 3D printers and smart speakers require new learning and consumption patterns, so they are radical.

stem: From the consumer's point of view, how new a product is depends on the degree of learning required to use it.
explanation: True. Newness can be judged from the company's view (new to the firm), the market's view (new to the market) or the consumer's view, where it depends on how much learning is required. That consumer view drives the minor, continuous and radical categories.

stem: PulseBand's new wrist tracker has users checking sleep and step data each morning and charging the band nightly. It changes their routine, but anyone who has used a phone app can figure it out. In terms of degree of innovation, this is a:
explanation: Wearable technology is Figure 8-5's example of a continuous innovation: it changes the consumer's normal routine without requiring totally new learning. It is more than minor (which requires no change at all) but less than radical (which requires new consumption patterns).
